To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
reducing black carbon emissions can improve air quality and human health, with the largest health impacts occurring in the regions with the largest emissions.
halving global black carbon emissions reduces outdoor population weighted average PM 2 5 by 542ng m 3 (1. 8%) and avoids 157000(120000–194000) annual premature human deaths.

halving BC emissions avoids 157 00 premature deaths globally (120–194 000, 95 % CI), with the vast majority of these occurring within the source regions, and that reducing BC emissions reduces surface air quality and avoids premature human mortality globally.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the health impacts of BC emissions globally and regionally, and the impacts of different sectors.
the impact of reducing black carbon (BC), which is a component of fine particle pollution (PM2.5), on human health.
the health impacts of BC, which has been a topic of considerable research interest and debate, but has been less well-studied than climate impacts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mortality impacts of halved global anthropogenic BC are substantial, with most impacts occurring within source regions.
the health benefits of BC emission reductions are substantial and should be considered in climate change mitigation policy.
reducing global anthropogenic BC concentrations would have a small but significant positive impact on global human health.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the global health impacts of BC emissions are substantial, but the regional impacts are highly variable and are dominated by the emissions in the regions themselves.

reducing BC emissions is an important strategy to improve air quality and reduce premature human mortality globally and that reducing BC and OC emissions simultaneously would be more effective than reducing either alone.

BC emissions are an important contributor to premature deaths globally, but that their impacts are highly regionalized and that the benefits of BC mitigation are likely much greater when considered together with other PM 2. 5 components, especially organic carbon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reducing BC emissions can improve air quality and human health, but these benefits vary substantially across regions and sectors.
the health benefits of BC mitigation are regionally and sectorally heterogeneous, and that BC mitigation strategies should be tailored to the region and sector of concern.
BC emissions are a large and tractable contributor to global PM 2. 5 and human mortality, especially in East Asia and South Asia.
